questions.question: Which statement best characterizes the GPU memory hierarchy relevant to training large models?
questions.choice_A: Host DRAM is on the GPU die and has the lowest latency; registers are off-chip and slow.
questions.choice_B: Registers and shared memory are on-chip with very low latency and limited capacity; HBM/global memory is larger but slower; transfers to host memory over PCIe/NVLink have much higher latency and lower effective bandwidth.
questions.choice_C: PCIe links provide lower latency than on-chip SRAM and are primarily used for caching activations.
questions.choice_D: Texture memory is the primary storage for model parameters during training.

questions.question: Why does sequence length strongly affect activation memory in Transformer training?
questions.choice_A: Because parameter tensors grow with sequence length, doubling $L$ doubles the number of weights.
questions.choice_B: Because the optimizer state must store a per-token copy of the parameters.
questions.choice_C: Because attention mechanisms can materialize attention scores with $O(L^2)$ memory within each layer, and non-attention activations scale roughly linearly with $L$ and batch size.
questions.choice_D: Because gradient tensors are discarded before the backward pass begins for long sequences.

questions.question: What is the core idea of gradient checkpointing (activation recomputation)?
questions.choice_A: Save only a subset of activations during the forward pass and recompute the missing ones during the backward pass to reduce peak memory usage at the cost of extra compute.
questions.choice_B: Compress parameters during the forward pass and decompress during the optimizer step to reduce disk I/O.
questions.choice_C: Shard layers across devices to eliminate all communication during backpropagation.
questions.choice_D: Replace backpropagation with second-order methods to reduce memory usage.

questions.question: In practical large-model training, which event often causes short-lived GPU memory spikes that can trigger out-of-memory errors if unaccounted for?
questions.choice_A: The initial CUDA context creation only.
questions.choice_B: Batch normalization in inference mode.
questions.choice_C: Saving checkpoints to disk.
questions.choice_D: Transitions between forward and backward passes, optimizer updates, and collective communication buffers that temporarily coexist with activations and gradients.

questions.question: What is the main benefit of offloading optimizer states (e.g., Adam moments) from GPU to CPU memory?
questions.choice_A: It eliminates the need to store gradients on any device.
questions.choice_B: It reduces GPU memory footprint significantly, enabling larger models or longer sequences at the cost of added host-device transfer overhead.
questions.choice_C: It increases arithmetic precision for parameter updates without any performance cost.
questions.choice_D: It removes the need for data parallelism.

questions.question: Which technique most directly helps hide host-to-device transfer latency when offloading or prefetching tensors?
questions.choice_A: Using larger batch sizes regardless of interconnect constraints.
questions.choice_B: Disabling CUDA streams to enforce strict synchronization.
questions.choice_C: Using pinned (page-locked) host memory and overlapping asynchronous memcpy with compute via CUDA streams/events.
questions.choice_D: Relying solely on filesystem caching for faster I/O.

questions.question: What is a defining characteristic of CUDA Unified Memory in the context of training large models?
questions.choice_A: It provides a single virtual address space with on-demand page migration between host and device, enabling oversubscription but risking page thrashing if access patterns lack locality.
questions.choice_B: It pins all program memory in GPU HBM at all times, preventing page faults.
questions.choice_C: It eliminates the need for any programmer control over data locality or prefetching.
questions.choice_D: It guarantees higher bandwidth than manually managed device memory transfers.

questions.question: When is activation checkpointing especially beneficial?
questions.choice_A: When the model is tiny and compute is the bottleneck.
questions.choice_B: When PCIe bandwidth is abundant and memory is plentiful.
questions.choice_C: When parameters dominate memory but activations are negligible.
questions.choice_D: When activations dominate peak memory (e.g., long sequences, deep networks) and extra compute for recomputation is acceptable.

questions.question: Which description best captures tensor (intra-layer) model parallelism?
questions.choice_A: Different pipeline stages host disjoint sets of layers.
questions.choice_B: Individual weight matrices are split across multiple GPUs so that one layer’s computation is distributed, requiring intra-layer communication to aggregate partial results.
questions.choice_C: Each GPU holds a full copy of the model and processes different batches.
questions.choice_D: All optimizer states are sharded across CPU threads on a single host.

questions.question: Which component often dominates GPU memory during training with long sequences and large batch sizes?
questions.choice_A: Parameter tensors only.
questions.choice_B: Dataloader worker buffers.
questions.choice_C: Intermediate activations (including attention-related tensors) kept for the backward pass.
questions.choice_D: Model code and kernel binaries.

questions.question: How does mixed-precision training typically affect memory usage?
questions.choice_A: Storing parameters and activations in lower precision (e.g., FP16/BF16) reduces memory, though some optimizers keep FP32 master weights unless sharded or offloaded.
questions.choice_B: It increases memory usage because tensor cores require duplication of tensors.
questions.choice_C: It has no effect on memory but only speeds up compute.
questions.choice_D: It removes the need to store gradients during backpropagation.

questions.question: What is a practical trade-off when choosing a checkpointing policy (which nodes to checkpoint) in deep networks?
questions.choice_A: Checkpointing more nodes always reduces both memory and compute.
questions.choice_B: Checkpointing fewer nodes strictly reduces compute with no memory impact.
questions.choice_C: Checkpoint placements are irrelevant because compilers erase all activations.
questions.choice_D: Aggressive checkpointing reduces peak memory by discarding more activations, but increases recomputation overhead; sparser checkpointing does the opposite.

questions.question: How can developers reduce page thrashing when using CUDA Unified Memory on large models?
questions.choice_A: Force all accesses to be random to distribute load across pages.
questions.choice_B: Use cudaMemPrefetchAsync to proactively move data to the device, provide memory advice for access patterns, and structure computation to improve spatial/temporal locality.
questions.choice_C: Disable NUMA awareness on the host.
questions.choice_D: Increase the number of CPU threads without modifying memory access patterns.

questions.question: Why does the interconnect (e.g., PCIe vs NVLink) matter when offloading tensors or optimizer states?
questions.choice_A: Because it determines numerical stability of floating-point operations.
questions.choice_B: Because it changes the size of GPU HBM.
questions.choice_C: Because bandwidth and latency dictate how much transfer can be overlapped with compute; slower interconnects make offloading more likely to bottleneck training.
questions.choice_D: Because it forces the use of unified virtual addressing.

questions.question: In the context of ZeRO-style optimizations for data-parallel training, which stage shards the parameters themselves across data-parallel ranks (not just gradients or optimizer states)?
questions.choice_A: Stage 0
questions.choice_B: Stage 1
questions.choice_C: Stage 2
questions.choice_D: Stage 3

questions.question: What is sequence parallelism trying to achieve in large-scale Transformer training?
questions.choice_A: Reduce activation memory by partitioning the sequence dimension across devices so each GPU materializes activations for fewer tokens.
questions.choice_B: Eliminate the attention mechanism to linearize memory.
questions.choice_C: Store all activations on CPU and stream them back on demand.
questions.choice_D: Shard only the embedding tables while keeping the rest replicated.

questions.question: What is a common effect of gradient accumulation on memory and performance?
questions.choice_A: It increases peak activation memory because it requires larger per-microbatch tensors.
questions.choice_B: It allows using smaller microbatches to reduce per-step activation memory while achieving a larger effective batch size over multiple accumulation steps, at the cost of more iterations per optimizer update.
questions.choice_C: It eliminates the need for all-reduce operations.
questions.choice_D: It moves optimizer states to GPU to speed up updates.

questions.question: Which runtime memory management strategy helps reduce allocator fragmentation and peak temporary memory during training?
questions.choice_A: Disabling caching allocators so every allocation goes to the OS/driver.
questions.choice_B: Allocating tensors with random sizes and lifetimes to avoid patterns.
questions.choice_C: Using a caching/pooling allocator with preallocation and reusing buffers (e.g., fused kernels and workspace reuse) to smooth allocation spikes.
questions.choice_D: Forcing all kernels to synchronize after each allocation.

questions.question: In pipeline parallelism, how does the number of micro-batches in flight affect activation memory per pipeline stage?
questions.choice_A: It does not affect memory because activations are recomputed each time.
questions.choice_B: Fewer micro-batches always increase activation memory footprint per stage.
questions.choice_C: Activation memory per stage is independent of the scheduling policy.
questions.choice_D: More micro-batches increase the number of concurrently stored activations per stage, raising peak activation memory; schedules trade off throughput (pipeline bubbles) versus memory.

questions.question: Given a system where GPUs are compute-underutilized but host-device bandwidth is limited, which approach is generally preferable to fit a larger model?
questions.choice_A: Favor activation recomputation (checkpointing) over offloading to avoid saturating the interconnect, trading extra compute for less data movement.
questions.choice_B: Favor offloading optimizer states and activations regardless of interconnect because bandwidth does not matter.
questions.choice_C: Disable mixed precision to reduce page faults.
questions.choice_D: Increase batch size until the interconnect saturates, then rely on UM page migration.
